Staples: Category Expansion Recommendation Analysis (Marketplace, Category Level)

The question

Staples does not sell everything a workplace buys. Some categories are missing, or carried only thinly, on Staples.com while Office Depot and the big marketplaces sell them. This PoC uses only the public category trees of Staples and five competitors to answer four questions:

  • Where are the gaps? Categories competitors carry that Staples does not (new), or carries much more thinly (deepen).
  • Are they within Staples' brand reach? Would a business, school, clinic, hotel or home-office buyer expect to find them at Staples? Antique collectables would fail this test.
  • Are they easy to open, and do they help Staples compete with the marketplaces?
  • Are they safe for Staples' own (1P) assortment? Would a marketplace there take sales from Staples' core shelves?

Brand reach, as defined for this PoC: workplace-first. A category is in reach when a workplace buyer mission plausibly includes it: office, home office, breakroom, janitorial and facilities, safety, school and classroom, healthcare, hospitality and foodservice, retail store and shipping, workspace décor, and commercial grounds. Residential lifestyle categories (bedding, kids' and teen bedrooms, home décor) are downgraded, not banned. Brand-unsafe categories (adult, weapons, tobacco, alcohol making, Rx and similar) are excluded outright.

The evidence: six category trees, every row accounted for

One adapter per retailer reads its tree into a common table. Office Depot is the closest B2B peer (the mirror). West Elm and Wayfair are the design lens; Wayfair also has a Professional (B2B) section. Amazon and Walmart are the scale marketplaces Staples competes with; Walmart also has Walmart for Business.

How we approached it

Nine stages in four phases: make the comparison fair, match every competitor shelf to Staples two independent ways, turn gaps into units and opportunities, then score and decide.

1 · Make the comparison fair
S0

Load, scope & reconcile

Six adapters build one table. A common department universe applies to every retailer, and merchandising pages, facets and headings are removed.

Every row → used / dropped / reference→L5 folded into L4→OD unmapped pages placed→Breakroom & classroom whitelist
OutputNode table, Row_Reconciliation sheet
Techpandas · openpyxl · regex adapters
S1

Represent every shelf

Each shelf is its label plus whatever path its retailer shows above it, with weights that decay going up the path (level-agnostic).

Own label 0.40 (Staples 0.70)→Ancestors, decaying→Headings skipped
OutputPath vectors; wording + thesaurus profiles
Techsentence-transformers · BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 (bake-off winner) · TF-IDF
2 · Match two independent ways
S2

Method V · vectors

The 50 nearest Staples shelves come from a Qdrant vector database (one collection per retailer), then they are re-scored on wording.

Top-50 by cosine→0.65 cosine + 0.35 wording→Best Staples shelf + score
OutputPer competitor shelf: matched / likely / gap
TechQdrant · NumPy fallback
S2

Method G · knowledge graph

The six trees form one graph. A match is more likely when the parents and children also match (similarity flooding). Adjacency is measured by Personalised PageRank from Staples' shelves.

Wording + thesaurus→3 rounds of flooding→PPR + sibling coverage
OutputPer competitor shelf: matched / likely / gap
TechNetworkX · Neo4j export
S3

Calibrate & verify

Thresholds are fitted per competitor on labelled rows. Hidden-department (ablation) negatives add realistic misses. Accuracy is reported both in-sample and cross-validated. Verified labels override the models.

τ: cost-weighted Youden J→Gap screen: 10th pct of carried→Verification loop
OutputEnsemble status per shelf
Techscikit-learn · labelled gold set
3 · From gaps to opportunities
S4

Build units

New: competitor subtrees whose shelves Staples mostly lacks, merged across competitors and searched in every competitor's collection. Deepen: Staples aisles where two or more competitors are at least twice as deep after size normalisation.

ENTER concepts→DEEPEN aisles→peer coverage k of 5
OutputUnits
Techagglomerative clustering
S5

Dock & roll up

Each unit docks into a Staples aisle by mission similarity plus graph/vector votes; catch-all departments are never docks. Consensus units roll up into category opportunities: one per zone and Staples department.

Mission-aware docking→zone × department opportunities→Watch list = 1 competitor
OutputOpportunities sheet
Techbge-base · graph votes
4 · Score & decide
S6

Score

Adjacency (AAS), cannibalisation risk (CRS), workplace brand fit (BFS), ease (EASE), peer consensus split into B2B and marketplace channels, and gap size, combined into one opportunity score O.

AAS · CRS · BFS→EASE · PC b2b / mkt · GS→O
OutputScores per unit and opportunity
TechNumPy
S7

Decide

The zone rule applies the safety screen first, then cannibalisation, then the brand gate, then adjacency. Residential categories drop one zone.

EXCLUDED → 1P-CORE GAP → REVIEW→OFF-BRAND gate→CURATE / VERTICAL EXT.→VERIFY
OutputZone, reason and action per unit
Techrules in poc_common.label_row
S8

Stress-test

500 runs re-draw the weights, jitter every threshold and the brand gate, and scale CRS by ±20%. A further 200 gold-label bootstraps re-fit the thresholds and re-test every gap verdict.

p_zone→p_top_n→p_gap
OutputStability per unit
TechNumPy

The scores

ScoreRangeMeaningHow it is built

Workplace buyer missions used for brand fit

Workplace: Office & business supplies · Office & home-office furniture · Technology for work · Breakroom & kitchen · Janitorial & facilities · Safety & security · School & classroom · Healthcare & clinics · Hospitality & foodservice · Retail store & shipping · Workspace decor & comfort · Commercial grounds & outdoor
Residential / leisure: Residential bedroom & bath · Home living & seasonal decor · Leisure, hobbies & sports · Backyard & garden living · Personal, fashion & novelty

The decision rule

ZoneRule (in this order)Action
EXCLUDEDBrand-safety term in the name or pathDo not pursue - fails the brand-safety screen (adult, weapons, tobacco, alcohol, Rx ...)
1P-CORE GAPCRS ≥ 60Fix in 1P merchandising - a marketplace here would cannibalise core
REVIEW40 ≤ CRS < 60Merchant decision - sits next to a 1P line
OFF-BRANDBFS < 35, or AAS < 40Pass - real gap, wrong store for Staples
CURATECRS < 40, BFS ≥ 35, AAS ≥ 60Open to marketplace sellers now (curated, design-led assortment)
VERTICAL EXTENSIONCRS < 40, BFS ≥ 35, 40 ≤ AAS < 60Phase 2 - enter through a vertical Staples already serves
VERIFYNew category not yet confirmed missing (mostly a soft gap, or peers' equivalents match a Staples shelf)Check first - Staples may already carry it under another name (findability)

A residential-lifestyle category, one closer to a residential mission than to any workplace mission, drops one zone: CURATE → VERTICAL EXTENSION → OFF-BRAND. Evidence grade: A = 3+ competitors and both methods agree; B = 2+ competitors or the methods agree; C = neither.

How good is the matching?

CompetitorLabelledCarried (random)V top-1V top-1 (CV)V AUCV acc. in-sampleV acc. (CV)G top-1G AUCG acc. (CV)
Office Depot21598%79%77%0.7870%62%73%0.7657%
West Elm12089%69%69%0.7559%62%52%0.7068%
Wayfair12082%60%58%0.7268%68%48%0.7170%
Amazon12079%54%54%0.7167%66%41%0.6958%
Walmart12087%58%59%0.6558%48%42%0.6550%

The encoder is chosen by a bake-off on the labelled rows (pooled top-1 after the rerank): st-base 67.0%, st 65.6%, tfidf 60.1%. Not available on this machine: spacy, wordllama. The thresholds re-calibrate for whichever encoder wins. The CV columns are held-out estimates: the encoder choice and τ are refitted without the fold being scored.

How reliable are the labels? A blind second pass re-labelled 60 labelled rows (12 per competitor) without seeing the original labels: 87% agreement, Cohen's κ = 0.65 ('substantial'). The original labels call a category carried more often (78% vs 72%). They accept a parent or neighbouring shelf (smart boards for interactive whiteboards, the dental department for dental anesthesia). The gold set is therefore slightly lenient, which makes the gap list conservative.

Finding for the next iteration: with the winning encoder, vector-only matching (68.0% pooled top-1) beats the 0.65 × cosine + 0.35 × wording rerank (67.0%). That weighting was tuned for V2's weaker word-vector encoder. It is kept here so it is not re-tuned on the same labels, and should be re-tuned on fresh labels.

Verification loop. Matching outside Office Depot is imperfect, so a model-flagged gap is not trusted on sight. Of 222 model-flagged shelves checked against the Staples tree, 121 were already sold under another name and 101 were real gaps. These checks are stored as labels that override the models, and they are excluded from threshold fitting (the model chose them, so they would bias τ). Concepts cleared this way form the VERIFY findability list.

How stable are the answers?

Two separate tests. Decision stability: in 500 runs the weights are re-drawn, every zone threshold and the brand gate are jittered by ±5, CRS is scaled by ±20% (coreness is a judgement proxy) and the penalty exponent varies from 0.5× to 2×. 31 of 57 recommended units keep their zone in at least 80% of runs. Matching stability: 200 bootstraps of the labelled rows re-fit each competitor's thresholds and re-test every member shelf of every new-category unit. 35 recommended units stay gaps in at least 80% of them (median over all new-category units: 100%).

What we found in the V2 analysis, and how V3 fixes it

V2 was a well-built pipeline (two matching engines, calibration, a verification loop), but it never tested the one thing the brief is about: whether a category is within the Staples brand's reach. Its adjacency score measures closeness to Staples' own category tree, which itself files patio furniture under Gift Shop › Professional Gifts › Compasses and has Décor and Expanded Assortment departments. Residential décor therefore looked 'adjacent'.

Assumptions and caveats

  • Category trees only. There is no sales, margin, search or traffic data. Demand is proxied by marketplace breadth (how many shelves Amazon and Walmart devote to a category, and Walmart's item counts). The code has a hook (external_signals.csv) for real demand signals.
  • Coreness is a judgement proxy (paper and office supplies 1.0, furniture 0.6, décor 0.1–0.2, +0.1 for departments in Staples' header navigation). It should be replaced with Staples' category sales bands, which is the most valuable single upgrade.
  • Brand fit is zero-shot, from sentence embeddings against written mission descriptions. The descriptions are editable in poc_common.py and should be reviewed with Staples merchants.
  • Labels were produced by the analysis team with Claude, against the Staples tree and live pages. They are marked for review with the Staples team.
  • Snapshots are from September 2026. Amazon and Wayfair publish no item counts, so they contribute breadth only. The Target tree is not used.
  • Category level only. Product and archetype gaps are covered by the separate product-level PoC.

Five calls for Staples

  1. Open now to curated marketplace sellers (CURATE): 11 opportunities. Lead with Retail Store Supplies: Sewing & Tailoring; Facilities: Adhesives, Sealants and Patching, Work Lights, Hardware; Arts & Crafts: Crafting; Furniture: Storage Furniture, Home & Office Tables. Each is next to an aisle Staples already runs, fits a workplace buyer mission, and puts little 1P revenue at risk.
  2. Phase 2, through a vertical Staples serves (VERTICAL EXTENSION): 10 opportunities, e.g. Furniture: Decor, Chairs & Seating; Facilities: Material Handling, Hardware; Tools, Parts & Supplies: Measuring & Leveling Tools, Power Tools, Hardware; Appliances & Kitchenware: Major Appliances, Kitchenware, Small Appliances. These are real gaps one step further from today's assortment; enter through education, hospitality, healthcare or facilities buyers.
  3. Keep in 1P and fix the assortment there: 22 opportunities, e.g. Coffee, Water & Snacks: Breakroom Appliances, Snacks & Food, Coffee …; Office Supplies: Desk Organizers & Accessories, Tape, Fasteners & Adhesives, Storage & Organization …; Furniture: Storage Furniture, Chairs & Seating, Chair Mats …. Competitors are deeper in Staples' own lines; a marketplace there would compete with Staples' shelf.
  4. Fix findability before buying assortment (VERIFY): 18 sub-categories, e.g. Ironing & Steaming, Reception Sets, Printmaking Inks, Anatomy Models, Boomboxes. They are probably sold already, under other names.
  5. Pass: 383 sub-categories are real gaps in the wrong store (e.g. Small Space Bedrooms, Hinges, Brittle, Caramel & Toffee, Latch Hook, Doormats); 42 fail the brand-safety screen outright.
